## Methods

Ethics Statement
Animal studies were conducted under the authorization of the Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee of the School of Basic Medical Sciences at Fudan University (approved number: 20210315-001). All animal experimental procedures strictly adhered to the International Ethical Guidelines and the National Institutes of Health Guide concerning the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.

Cell lines and virus
Human lung epithelial cell A549, mouse macrophage J774A.1, transformed human liver epithelial-2 (THLE-2), and the African green monkey kidney epithelial cell Vero E6 cell lines were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). All cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) containing 10% FBS and 1% Pen/Strep, and incubated at 37 °C under 5% (v/v) CO2 atmosphere. SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.5.2 variant came from and was conducted in Biosafety Level 3 (BSL3) Laboratory at Shanghai Medical College, Fudan University.

Enzymatic assays
A fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based assay was adopted to quantitatively determine the inhibitory activity of compounds against Mpro and its mutants, with an internally quenched fluorogenic peptidyl substrate Dabcyl-KTSAVLQSGFRKME-Edans (Beyotime) using wavelengths of 340 nm and 490 nm for excitation and emission, respectively 19,61. To determine enzymatic parameters, Mpro were initially diluted in assay buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 50 mM NaCl, 0.1 mM EDTA, pH 7.4) to specified concentrations. Specifically, the working concentrations were 100 nM for wild-type (WT) SARS-CoV-2 Mpro and its 15N-labelled protein as well as SARS-CoV-1 Mpro, 400 nM for MERS-CoV Mpro, 500 nM for three mutants including M49L/E166A, L50F/E166A/L167F and L50F/E166V, and 1600 nM for H163A mutant of SARS-CoV-2 Mpro. Different concentrations of fluorescent substrate were added into the diluted Mpro. Fluorescence intensities were kinetically monitored by a Spark® multifunctional plate reader (Tecan). Initial velocities were referred as the slopes calculated from fitting the linear portion of the curves to a straight line. A standard curve was generated using Edans, then the time-dependent changes in fluorescence signals of each sample were converted to the catalytic velocity using the unit of nM/s. Parameters including Km, kcat and Vmax were calculated using nonlinear regression fitting by GraphPad Prism 8.0 according to Michaelis-Menten equation.

For determining inhibition constants (Ki), Mpro were diluted in assay buffer to working concentrations (100 nM for WT Mpro of SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2, 400 nM for MERS-CoV Mpro, L50F/E166A/L167F and L50F/E166V mutants, and 200 nM for M49L/E166A mutant as well as 1600 nM for H163A mutant). Different concentrations of compounds were then added into the diluted Mpro, and incubated at 37 °C for 5 min. Fluorescence intensities were kinetically monitored by a Spark® multifunctional plate reader (Tecan) after addition of fluorescent substrate (10 μM). The initial velocities were referred as the slopes calculated from fitting the linear portion of the curves to a straight line. Enzymatic activities were characterized by percent velocities in presence of different concentrations of compounds. Ki values were obtained via fitting to the Morrison equation by GraphPad Prism 8.0.

Cytotoxicity assays
Cell lines including A549, J774A.1, THLE-2 and Vero E6 were adopted to evaluate in vitro cytotoxic profiles of tested compounds. Specifically, these cells were plated in 96-well plates with a cell density of 20,000 cells per well, respectively, and incubated at 37 °C overnight. Tested compounds with concentrations ranging from 0.195 to 50 μM were added into cell medium, and the untreated cells cultured in fresh medium were set as control groups. After 24-hour incubation, 10 μL of WST-1 (Beyotime) was added into each well and incubated for 60 min at 37 °C. The optical density for each well was determined by microplate reader at 450 nm (OD450). The assay was biologically repeated for three times. Percent survival (%) of cells was calculated relative to control groups.

In vivo acute toxicity assays
Healthy 8- to 12-week-old male BALB/c mice (17~22 g) were orally administered with test compounds (NTV, FD3-32, and FD3-33) in a low (100 mg/kg), medium (300 mg/kg), or high (900 mg/kg) dosage, respectively. Mice were clinically observed for 7 days after administration, and the body weights were recorded every day. At the end of the experiment, blood samples collected from three mice per group were subjected for detection of alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), creatinine (CREA), and urea nitrogen (BUN).

Pharmacokinetic analysis
NTV, FD3-32, FD3-33, ITV and FD3-36 were subjected to pharmacokinetic analysis via intravenous injection (i.v.) or oral administration (p.o.), respectively. 8- to 12-week-old male BALB/c mice were administered with a single dose of 20 mg/kg (i.v.) and 2 mg/kg (p.o.) compounds in saline containing 5% DMSO, 20% HP-β-CD, and 15% HS-15. Blood samples were collected at specified time points (0.083, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 h for i.v for all tested compounds.; 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 24 h for p.o. for NTV, FD3-32 and FD3-33; 0.083, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 24 h for p.o. for ITV and FD3-36) pose-dose, and subsequently centrifuged at 3000 ×g at 4°C for 10 min. Blood samples retrieved from healthy mice were diluted in saline to prepare standard curves by adding specified concentrations (5, 10, 20, 50, 200, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000 ng/mL) of tested compounds. Supernatants of blood samples were analyzed by LC-MS/MS to determine plasma drug concentrations. A Waters Acquity Premier UPLC-Xevo TQ Absolute equipped with a ACQUITY Premier BEH C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm, 1.7 μm) were employed for separation and quantification of tested compounds with a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min with mobile phase A (0.2% formic acid in ddH2O) and mobile phase B (acetonitrile). Gradient: 0-0.5 min, 10% solvent B; 0.5-1.2 min, 10-90% solvent B; 1.2-1.7 min, 90% solvent B; 1.7-1.8 min, 90-10% solvent B; 1.8-2.5 min, 10% solvent B. The average plasma concentration and standard deviation at each time point were calculated, and PKSolver was employed to fit the pharmacokinetic parameters using a non-compartmental model 62.

Cellular antiviral assays
Vero E6 cells were plated in 96-well plates with a cell density of 20,000 cells per well, and cultured overnight at 37 °C in DMEM medium plus 10% FBS and 1% Pen/Strep. SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.5.2 variant (100 TCID50) was then added in the presence or absence of NTV, FD3-32, FD3-33, ITV, or FD3-36 at specified concentrations in DMEM medium plus 2% FBS and 1% Pen/Strep, and the resultant cell plates were placed at 37 °C and cultured for 48 h. For characterizing sensitivity of tested inhibitors to P-gp-mediated efflux, cellular antiviral assays were additionally conducted in the presence and absence of 2 μM CP-100356 (a standard P-gp inhibitor) 13,51. Supernatants were collected from Vero E6 cell culture for RT-qPCR analysis using specific primers of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein genes. The cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min, followed by permeabilization with 0.2 % Triton X-100 for 30 min, which were then stained with rabbit anti-SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein antibody (Sino Biological) and Rhodamine-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Proteintech). After immunofluorescence staining, expression and distribution of nucleocapsid protein in Vero E6 cells were imaged by BZ-X810 Fluorescence Microscope (KEYENCE). Semi-quantification of immunofluorescence images was performed by Image J.

In vivo antiviral assays
All animal experiments involving SARS-CoV-2 infection were performed within a certified animal biosafety level 3 (BSL3) laboratory at Shanghai Medical College, Fudan University. All animal studies were conducted under the authorization of the Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee of the School of Basic Medical Sciences at Fudan University (approved number: 20210315-001). Ten to fourteen-week-old male humanized C57BL6/S mice (CAG-hACE2-IRES-ALuc-Tg) were purchased from Shanghai Model Organisms, and then housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) facility of BSL3 laboratory in Fudan University in a 12-h light-dark cycle, under the condition with ad libitum access to irradiation sterilized rodent diet and aseptic water. Mice were divided into four groups (six mice per group) with initial anesthetization by 20 μL/g avertin (Nanjing Aibei Biotechnology), and subsequently challenged intranasally with ~5000 PFUs of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.5.2 in a total volume of 40 μL DMEM. Additional three mice without infection were defined as a mock group. Therapeutic candidates (NTV, FD3-32, and FD3-33) plus RTV were formulated by dissolving in 0.5% methylcellulose solution containing 2% Tween-80 to satisfy requirements of oral administration. After two-hour infection, mice were orally administrated with 200 mg/kg NTV plus 50 mg/kg RTV twice a day (b.i.d.), or 200 mg/kg FD3-32/FD3-33 plus 50 mg/kg RTV once a day (q.d.). All mice were sacrificed after three-day treatments; lung and brain were collected for RT-qPCR assay to quantify loads of viral RNA; owing to time limit of BSL3, only three brain tissues from NTV group had been collected for quantifying viral RNA. Besides, parts of lung tissues were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and further submitted to immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analysis for visualize/quantify the distribution and expression of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein. H&E staining was conducted to show the histopathological alterations of lung tissues.

To demonstrate therapeutic efficacy of FD3-32 as a monotherapy, we additionally performed an in vivo antiviral assay. Ten to fourteen-week-old male humanized C57BL6/S mice (CAG-hACE2-IRES-Luc-Tg) were divided into three groups (six mice per group) with initial anesthetization by 20 μL/g avertin (Nanjing Aibei Biotechnology), and subsequently challenged intranasally with ~5000 PFUs of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.5.2 in a total volume of 40 μL DMEM. Therapeutic candidates including FD3-32 alone or NTV plus RTV were also formulated by dissolving in 0.5% methylcellulose solution containing 2% Tween-80. After two-hour infection, infected mice were orally administrated with 200 mg/kg FD3-32 alone, or 200 mg/kg NTV plus 50 mg/kg RTV, or vehicle with equal volume, twice a day (b.i.d.). All mice were sacrificed after three-day treatments; bronchus, lung and brain were collected for RT-qPCR assay to quantify loads of viral RNA. Besides, tissues of lung were additionally fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, and were further submitted to immunohistochemical and immunofluorescent analysis of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein. H&E analysis was also performed to present the histopathological alterations of lung tissues from our tested mice. The same protocols were employed for determining the in vivo therapeutic efficacy of FD3-36 monotherapy against Omicron BA.5.2 infection, in comparison to NTV co-administrating RTV. Due to unexpected death of two mice before infecting virus, the data from 5 mice in the FD3-36 and NTV+RTV groups were ultimately collected. Histopathological lung injury was assessed and scored on a 5-point scale based on the exudation and alveolar membrane thickening: 0, minimal damage; 1, mild damage; 2, moderate damage; 3, severe damage; and 4, maximal damage 63.

Computational methods
Molecular docking
Virtual screening: A crystal structure of SARS-CoV-2 Mpro in complex with a non-covalent inhibitor X77 (PDB ID: 6W63) was employed for all docking calculations in this study. The crystal structure was then prepared via protonation at pH 7.0 by Epik and PROPKA in Maestro. According to a previous publication that used the same crystal structure (PDB: 6W63) for virtual screening 61, histidine residues including His41, His163, His164, His172, and His246 were modeled as Nε-protonated, whereas His64 and His80 were modeled as Nδ-protonated. Crystallographic waters within 3.0 Å from the ligand were retained otherwise removed from the structure. And then the structure was submitted to energy-minimization optimization with OPLS4 force field. Receptor Grid files were generated by applying a cube box with a center of inherent ligand and a size of 20 Å × 20 Å × 20 Å, by using Receptor Grid Generation. Approximately 3 million molecules from the Enamine library (comprising the Advanced, Functional, HTS, and Premium collections, downloaded in December 2021) were initially filtered using Lipinski's rule of five. A high throughput docking campaign was conducted using Schrödinger2021-2 by module of Virtual Screening Workflow on AMD CPU with 128 cores, 256 threads, which used CPU core time of ~120h. The van der Waals scaling was set to 0.8 for the nonpolar atoms of the ligand, and the partial charge cutoff was set to 0.15. Three level docking algorithms with differential accuracy, including HTVS, SP and XP, were applied to perform docking calculations, with 10% compounds reserved after each step’s computation. The final output of hit compounds after multiple docking was re-scored by Prime MM-GBSA to calculate binding free energy.

Induced fit docking: Predicted docking poses of our synthetic inhibitors in complex with Mpro were generated by Schrödinger software package. Receptor was prepared using the conditions consistent with those of virtual screening. LigPrep module was employed to calculate the molecular mechanic parameters of our compounds with OPLS4 force field, and generate states at pH 7.0 by Epik. Non-covalent docking was performed by using Induced Fit Docking module. Receptor Grid files were generated by applying a cube box with a center of inherent ligand and a size of 20 Å × 20 Å × 20 Å. The van der Waals scaling was set to 0.5 for the nonpolar atoms of the receptor and ligand, and the maximum number of poses was set to 20. Multi-thread parallel calculation was employed for individual compound by assigning 20 AMD CPU cores.

Covalent docking: Complexes of our peptidomimetic covalent inhibitors with Mpro were predicted by using the Covalent Docking module of Schrödinger software package. Preparation of receptor and ligands was conducted as previously described. Mass of center of inherent ligand was adopted as the centroid of cube box with a size of 20 Å × 20 Å × 20 Å. Reaction type between the -SH of C145 and -CN of our compounds was set to nucleophilic addition to a triple bond. ~20 AMD CPU cores were assigned to perform the covalent docking per compounds.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations
Crystal structures of Mpro in complex with NTV (PDB ID: 7RFS) and peptidyl substrate (PDB ID: 7DVP) 8,13, co-crystal structure of FD6-31/Mpro complex and those docking complexes of our synthetic compounds binding to Mpro were initially imported to PyMOL for removing hydrogens. Chemical structures of ligands were created by Chem3D, were then optimized, and the partial atomic charges were calculated by AM1-BCC method via Antechamber module in Amber20 to obtain the molecular mechanics parameters of small molecules 64. For complexes of covalent inhibitors, parameters of the non-canonical bond formed in the corresponding reactive site should be manually added to the force field files. The molecular mechanic parameters from ff19SB and GAFF2 force field were then assigned to these complexes which were subsequently neutralized by adding potassium/chlorine counter ions and solvated in a cuboid box of transferable interatomic potential with three points model (TIP3P) water molecules with solvent layers 12.0 Å between solute surface and box edges, via LEaP module 65,66. In parallel with the volume of box, specific counts of potassium/chlorine ions were added to achieve the physiological concentration (150 mM) of KCl. Overall, system setup parameters for all-atom MD simulations involved in this study were provided in Table S4. All MD simulations were conducted by using Amber20. The SHAKE algorithm was employed to restrict all covalent bonds involving hydrogen atoms. The pmemd.MPI module was used to perform the minimization, heat, density and equilibration of these solvated complexes through parallel computation with assignation of 64 AMD CPU cores. The solvent and ions were optimized using 10000 steps of steepest descent minimization and 10000 steps of conjugated gradient minimization with protein backbone restrained by 25 kcal mol-1Å-2. The systems were further undergone three steps of energy minimizations by 5000-step steepest descent and 5000-step conjugated gradient minimizations with restrain of backbone Cα atoms by 25, 10, and 5 kcal mol-1Å-2, respectively. Last, the systems were fully relaxed by 10000-step of steepest descent and 10000-step conjugated gradient minimizations without any restraint, thus to remove unfavorable contacts. After minimizations, the systems were heated from 0 K to 300 K in 160-ps timescale and maintained 300 K for 40 ps, by using Langevin dynamics at a constant volume, with a time step of 2 fs. A 200-ps density equilibration was then performed to optimize the heated system which was subsequently undergone two steps of NPT (T = 300 K, P = 1 atm) equilibration with or without backbone restrain for total 200 ps. Finally, these systems were respectively submitted to a 100-ns NPT (T = 300 K, P = 1 atm) production MD simulation with isotropic pressure scaling by using the pmemd.cuda module. Production simulations for each setting were run triplicate. MD trajectories were analyzed by employing CPPTRAJ to extract the RMSD and monitor hydrogen bonds. Conformations at specific frames were exported by using CPPTRAJ, and visualized by PyMOL. MMPBSA.py.MPI module was used to calculate the gibbs free energy change (ΔG) between ligands and Mpro according to the MM/GBSA approach, and the ΔG was further decomposed into the contributions of each residue in Mpro 67. Besides, MMPBSA.py.MPI was also used to run alanine scanning to calculate the ΔΔG after single mutation of residues in Mpro. All production simulations in this study were run for three times to obtain three independent trajectories. All quantitative data in MD simulations were analyzed and visualized by GraphPad Prism 8.0.

Cheminformatics
Enamine library computationally screened against Mpro finally identified a molecular set containing 10847 candidates. To further elucidate chemical features of these compounds to bind receptor, chemical spaces were explored via an extensive effort of RDKit. The molecular set in SDF file was initially imported and adjusted the order of individual compound randomly. Morgan fingerprints were then computed in a radius of 2, and the number of bits was set to 2048 68. Tanimoto similarity was calculated using Morgan fingerprints as input; and Tanimoto distance represented as 1-Tanimoto similarity, was used to construct distance matrix that subsequently transferred to numpy array 68. Compounds were thus clustered to ten groups based on the array of Tanimoto distances by adopting Ward method, and were further visualized as two-dimensional (2D) chemical space by principal components analysis (PCA). The compounds with the best MM/GBSA binding free energy among each group were automatically picked out. RDKit was also employed to search the compounds with substructures of specified aromatic nitrogen heterocycles through matching the simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) string. 2D chemical spaces were rendered by Seaborn to present the density of molecular distributions, in which the compounds with specified aromatic nitrogen heterocycles were scattered. Potential candidates in scattered compounds exhibited favorable fitting to Mpro were picked out in terms of the interactions with H163, H41, and G143.

Expression and purification of SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2, and MERS-CoV Mpro and SARS-CoV-2 Mpro E166X mutants
The DNA sequences encoding Mpro of SARS-CoV (nsp5, NCBI RefSeq NC_004718.3), MERS-CoV (nsp5, NCBI RefSeq NC_019843.3), and SARS-CoV-2 (GenBank: MN908947.3) was synthesized with codon optimization for expression in E. coli by TSINGKE, and constructed into the vector of pET28a-SUMO by homologous recombination. The M49L/E166A mutation plasmid was constructed based on above plasmid of wild-type Mpro as template, with the mutation primers as following:
F-M49L: AGATCTGCTGAATCCGAATTATGAAG;
R-M49L: CAGCAGATCTTCACTCGTGC;
F-E166A: CACATGGCACTGCCGACCG;
R-E166A: CAGTGCCATGTGATGCATATAACAAAAGCTC.

Expression vectors of SARS-CoV-2 mutants including L50F/E166V and L50F/E166Q/L167F were synthesized by DETAIBIO, and then constructed into the vector pET30a by homologous recombination. Abovementioned vectors were respectively transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3). A colony of the bacteria was inoculated into 10 mL of LB broth containing 100 μg/mL kanamycin, and cultured overnight at 200 rpm, 37 °C. The overnight inoculum was sub-cultured with ratio of 1:100 for ~150 min until OD600 ≈ 0.6-0.8, then 1 mM IPTG was added for induction of protein expression and incubated overnight at 180 rpm and 16 °C. The bacteria were resuspended in the binding buffer (Tris/HCl pH 8.4+20 mM Imidazole) equivalent to one-thirtieth of the volume of the raw induced bacterial suspension, and then lysed by ultra-high pressure microjet homogenizer at ~1050 bar and 6 °C for 15 min. After centrifuging the bacterial lysate at 12000 ×g for 20 min, the fusion protein existed in the supernatant of the bacterial lysate. The fusion protein was purified by Ni-NTA column (His-Trap FF5ml) with a protein purifier (BIO-RAD NGC Quest 10plus). Before purification, 10 CVs (column volumes) of the binding buffer were used to equilibrate the column at 5 mL/min, and then 15 mL of the sample was loaded at 3 mL/min. After that, 15 CVs of binding buffer were used to wash the non-specific miscellaneous proteins at 5 mL/min. Finally, the protein was eluted by the elution buffer (Tris/HCl pH 8.4+500 mM Imidazole) at a 0-60% gradience for 13 CVs. The final products of mutants L50F/E166V and L50F/E166A/L167F were obtained after eluting of Ni-NTA column. To remove the His6-Sumo tag at the N-terminus of Mpro and Mpro M49L/E166A mutant, the fusion protein was cut by the Sumo Protease (Smart-Lifesciences, China) as instructed by the manufacturer overnight at 4 °C. And the resultant samples were dialyzed overnight at 4 °C against 4 L of fresh binding buffer, the His6-SUMO tag and SUMO protease were both removed when the sample was passed through the Ni-NTA column (His-Trap FF5ml). These final products of proteins were verified by LC-MS, and were concentrated up to about 8 mg/ml, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and then stored at -80°C until used.

15N-labelled SARS-CoV-2 Mpro expression and purification
A colony of the E. coli BL21(DE3) (pET28a-SUMO-Mpro) was inoculated into 10 ml M9 broth containing 100 μg/ml kanamycin, using 15N-NH4Cl (1g/L) as nitrogen source, and cultured at 200 rpm, 37°C overnight. The overnight inoculum was 1:100 sub-cultured for ~150 min until OD600 ≈ 0.6-0.8, then 1 mM IPTG was added for induction of protein expression. The expression was induced at 180 rpm 37 °C for 3 h and then 16 °C overnight. The bacteria were resuspended in the binding buffer (Tris/HCl pH 8.4+20 mM Imidazole) equivalent to one-thirtieth of the volume of the raw induced bacterial suspension, and then lysed by ultra-high pressure microjet homogenizer at ~1050 bar and 6 °C for 15 min. After centrifuging the bacterial lysate at 12000 ×g for 20 min, the fusion protein existed in the supernatant of the bacterial lysate. The fusion protein was purified by Ni-NTA column (His-Trap FF5ml) with a protein purifier (BIO-RAD NGC Quest 10plus). Before purification, 10 CVs (column volumes) of the binding buffer were used to equilibrate the column at 5 mL/min, and then 15 mL of the sample was loaded at 3 mL/min. After that, 15 CVs of binding buffer were used to wash the non-specific miscellaneous proteins at 5 mL/min. Finally, the protein was eluted by the elution buffer (Tris/HCl pH 8.4+500 mM Imidazole) at a 0-60% gradience for 13 CVs. Then they were added into the dialysis bag, and by dialyzing the sample overnight at 4°C against 3 L of fresh binding buffer with 5 mM β-mercaptoethanol, The His6-SUMO tag and SUMO protease were both removed when the sample was passed through a HisTrap FF5ml column (Cytiva). The flow-through containing the native Mpro was dialyzed (cut-off 6-8 kDa) twice at 4 °C against 4 L of NMR buffer (100 mM NaPi, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 2 mM DTT, pH 6.8). The protein was verified by LC-MS, the products were concentrated up to about 8 mg/ml, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and then stored at -80 °C until used.

Electrospray ionization time-of-flight (ESI-TOF) mass spectrometer Assay
To validate the covalent-inhibition mechanism, purified wild-type (WT) Mpro (15 μM) were mixed with FD3-6, FD3-9, FD3-32 and FD3-33 respectively, at a molar ratio of 4:1 (Mpro:inhibitor), and incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. Besides, for characterizing dose-response relationships, purified WT Mpro, M49L/E166A mutant, L50F/E166V mutant and L50F/E166A/L167F mutant (15 μM) were incubated with NTV or FD3-33 at molar ratios ranging from 1:5 to 1:0.039 (Mpro:inhibitor), respectively, and incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. All samples were prepared with a single biological replicate and were then injected into LC-MS system (Agilent HPLC Infinity II 1290 system coupled with a TOF 6230 detector) by using XBridge® Protein BEH C4 column (2.1 mm × 150 mm, 3.5 μm) for separation with a flow rate of 0.4 mL/min with solvent A (0.1% (v/v) TFA in Milli-Q water) and solvent B (0.1% (v/v) TFA in acetonitrile). The initial gradient of 5% solvent B was maintained for 2 min, followed by a gradual increase to 95% for 15 min and maintained for 2 min, and finally back to 5% solvent that maintained for 2 min. Samples went through column were automatically detected by ESI-TOF real time to reflect the relative abundances of Mpro as well as the covalent complexes of Mpro with inhibitors. The exact mass was calculated by deconvoluting molecular ion peaks in ESI-TOF spectra. MS parameters: Gas Temp, 300 °C; Drying Gas, 5 L/min; Nebulizer, 40 psi; Sheath Gas Temp, 325 °C; Sheath Gas Flow, 11 L/min; VCap, 3500 V.

Crystallization, data collection, structure determination, and refinement
SARS-CoV-2 Mpro protein (16 mg/ml) was preincubated with 100 mM FD6-31 (in 100% DMSO) for a molar ratio of approximately 1:3, for 12-18 h at 4 °C. The complex was then passed through a 0.22 μM cellulose-acetate spin filter and set up for crystallization using crystallization robot (Art Robbins Instruments). Each drop consisted of 0.6 μL of protein solution and 0.6 μL of reservoir solution (0.1 M Bis-Tris 6.5, 20% PEG5000MME) and was equilibrated against 80 μL of reservoir solution at 16 °C for 5–7 days to allow crystals to grow. Large crystals were flash cooled in liquid nitrogen after being passed through a cryoprotectant consisting of reservoir solution containing 20% ethylene glycol. The diffraction data were collected using a single crystal at 100 K with a wavelength of 0.979 Å at beamline BL10U2 of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF) and were integrated and scaled using HKL2000. The structure was solved by molecular replacement using the Mpro complex structure (PDB code: 7VIC) as the search model in the program Molrep. Iterative refinements of the structure model were carried out using Coot and Refmac5. The stereochemical quality of the final model was assessed using MolProbity. The statistics of the data collection and structural refinement are listed in Table S1. The coordinate and structural factors of the Mpro-6-31 complex have been deposited in Protein Data Bank (PDB) under the accession code 9L13.

2D-NMR characterization
All NMR samples were prepared in an NMR buffer containing 100 mM NaPi (pH 6.8), 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 2 mM DTT, and 10% D2O. The final concentration of Mpro were approximately 500 μM. Compounds were titrated from a stock solution to protein at a molar ratio of 2:1. All samples were prepared with a single biological replicate. All NMR spectra were collected at 298.15 K on a Bruker Avance III HD 800 MHz spectrometer equipped with 1H-13C-15N RT-probe. The operating frequencies were 800 MHz for 1H, 201 MHz for 13C, and 80 MHz for 15N. 2D [15N, 1H] TROSY-HSQC spectra were acquired by using the standard Bruker pulse sequence trosyetf3gpsi.2. The spectral widths were set to 13.9486 ppm (F2/1H) and 35.0000 ppm (F1/15N). A total of 1024 complex data points were collected in the direct dimension (F2), and 160 complex increments were collected in the indirect dimension (F1). The spectrum was accumulated with 256 scans per increment. Data were collected and processed by Topspin 4.4.1, and analyzed by CCPNMR3.2.2. Partial assignments were performed through superimposing collected spectra with previously reported spectra 43,44. Combined chemical shift deviations (CCSD) were adopted as a measure of assignment reliability/ambiguity. CCSD were computed for assigned signals in [1H, 15N] TROSY-HSQC spectra according to Eq.1 (below) 69,70:
CCSD = √0.5×[(δH-δH,ref)2 + (αδN-αδN,ref)2] (1)

Differential scanning fluorimetry
Thermal-shift profiles of WT Mpro and mutants in the presence and absence of inhibitors were determined by employing a fluorescence-based thermal shift assay as previously reported 48-50. Purified WT Mpro and resistant mutants including M49L/E166A, L50F/E166V, and L50F/E166A/L167F were diluted in buffer containing 40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.4) and 150 mM NaCl to a final concentration of 10 μM. For characterizing influence of inhibitors to thermal profiles, NTV and FD3-33 were added to each Mpro in a final concentration of 10 μM, respectively, and incubated at 25 °C for 10 min. After addition of SYPRO Orange dye (Sigma-Aldrich, final concentration = 20×), the melting curves and melting temperatures (Tm) were thus determined by detecting fluorescent intensity (RFU) of SYRPRO Orange at 490/530 nm excitation/emission wavelengths with heating from 25°C to 95 °C with increment of 0.5 °C (Bio-Rad CFX Connect Real-Time PCR System, FRET mode). The -d(RFU)/dT was plotted against temperature (T), and the minimal signal of the peak was used to define Tm.

Medicinal chemistry
Details on medicinal chemistry including synthesis and compound characterization used in this study can be found in the Supplementary Information.

Statistics and reproducibility
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. The investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. Data are presented as mean ± SD or mean ± SEM as specified. The statistical comparisons between two groups were analyzed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test, and comparisons among multiple groups were performed by two-sided one-way ANOVA or two-way ANOVA. Differences were considered statistically significant when P < 0.05. The Ki values were calculated by fitting to the Morrison equation, while the IC50 values were obtained by fitting to the four-parameter dose-response model in GraphPad Prism 8.
review_generation.target:
### Reviewer 1

Luo et al reported a systematic design strategy to improve next-generation SARS-CoV-2 Mpro targeted inhibitors with a
highly significant improvement in antiviral potency, toxicity, and pharmacokinetics profiles over Paxlovid (NTV). The authors
elegantly provided a rationale for how they strategize the design to principally avoid the interaction of the γ-lactam ring with
F140, H163, and E166, which were found to stabilize the interaction of NTV with Mpro. Mutations of H163 and E166 also
confer resistance to NTV. The study was done systematically, starting with virtual screening, MD simulations, NMR, X-ray
crystallography, in vitro and in vivo antiviral assays, SAR, and pharmacokinetics measurements. The best compounds, FD3-
32, FD3-33, and FD3-36, showed significant improvement in all aspects compared to NTV and a recent clinical candidate,
Ibuzatrelvir (ITV). The major achievement is that, unlike NTV, which requires pretreatment with Ritonavir (RTV) for its
efficacy, the newly developed compounds can be used as monotherapy like ITV.
Overall, this is an outstanding study that has significantly advanced NTV and
ITV. The study will pave the way for designing other antivirals using similar
strategies. The authors also presented the methodology in detail with detailed
statistical analyses.
However, the author should address the possibility of H163 mutations by the
newly designed compounds since the new compounds principally bind to H163,
and it was shown that the H163A mutation completely abolishes the catalytic
activity of Mpro. To make this contribution even more impactful, the authors
should try to generate laboratory-evolved mutations by 1-2 of the most active
and pharmacologically improved compounds.

### Reviewer 2

This work presents the discovery and optimization of a lead compounds, designed to circumvent two limitations of the
currently available therapeutic, Paxlovid. 1) The requirement of co-administration with Ritonavir and 2) The susceptibility of
nirmatrelvir to mutations at E166.
The paper first starts with the screening of a virtual library to discover a replacement for the γ-lactam group that occupies the
S1 pocket of Mpro. Binders were confirmed by chemical-shift perturbation using NMR, a crystal structure of one compound
(FD6-31) with Mpro to confirm the binding pose, molecular dynamics simulations of this complex and a virtual alanine scan
to confirm the importance of contacting residues. This initial part of the study concluded that the iso-quinoline is an
acceptable substituent to bind the S1 pocket of Mpro.
This has previously been observed "An increase in potency was unlocked by replacing pyridine with isoquinoline, which
picks up additional hydrophobic interactions with N142. "Open science discovery of potent noncovalent SARS-CoV-2 main
protease inhibitors. Science382,eabo7201(2023).DOI:10.1126/science.abo7201
Subsequent experiments took this observation and replaced the γ-lactam of nirmatrelvir with an iso-quinoline and used this
as a base to perform SAR. Activity was measured with enzymatic assays with recombinant protein, while optimizing other
substituents to generate high affinity compounds that could be tested against variants of Mpro that escape nirmatrelvir. The
replacement of the γ-lactam with iso-quinoline enabled subsequent compounds to be less sensitive to tested E166 variants
and I believe this is novel.
Although virtual screening and validation was performed, the main crux of work is a SAR study on nirmatrelvir. Other studies
involving nirmatrelvir SAR have been published - eg: Arun K. Ghosh, et al,. Exploration of P1 and P4 modifications of
nirmatrelvir: Design, synthesis, biological evaluation, and X-ray structural studies of SARS-CoV-2 Mpro inhibitors, European
Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, Volume 267, 2024. This detracts from the overall novelty of the work, as novel candidates
from the virtual screen were not pursued.
The work then extends further into cellular and in vivo models of infection. The authors claim that they have identified
compounds that are more potent than nirmatrelvir, do not need to be co-administered with ritonavir. They claim their
compounds have comparable PK properties to Paxlovid and are also active against SARS1 and MERS.
The claim that the designed inhibitors are 3 orders of magnitude more potent than nirmatrelvir is misleading. Most readers
would assume this means a compound with 1000-fold better binding affinity, but this is likely due to altered efflux in the
cellular assay, which were performed without P-gp efflux inhibitors. Testing compounds with and without P-gp inhibitors
should be done if specific claims about sensitivity to efflux via this route are made. A supplementary dataset should be
provided that contains the compounds with Ki values against Mpro wildtype and Mpro variants.
It is difficult to assess whether the in vivo data shows a benefit of the new compounds compared to Paxlovid. A central claim
of the paper is that ritonavir is not required for the new compounds, but this is not tested head-to-head. Figure 5D shows an
experiment with nirmatrelvir, FD3-32, FD3-33 all with ritonavir. This shows the FD3-x compounds as performing better than
nirmatrelvir, however, this differentiating feature is lost in the experiment in Figure 5K where FD3.32 is tested without
ritonavir.
It is well known that nirmatrelvir pharmacokinetics are poor in the absence of ritonavir. Nirmatrelvir and the compounds
tested in the paper all show poor serum half-life. FD3.32 is better, but still has a half-life of less than an hour, suggesting that
modification of the compounds has probably not addressed the issue requiring co-administration of ritonavir. Head-to-head
comparison of PK +/- ritonavir would determine how dependent the PK properties are on CYP3A/P-gp-mediated clearance.
These arguments could be strengthened if these points are addressed.
Major points:
1) The statistical treatment of the data is weak. When discussing Ki values in the section exploring the structure activity
relationship, claims such as "However, iso-quinoline replacement of γ-lactam improved inhibitory activity of FD3-6 over NTV
by 40%" can't be supported unless multiple biological replicates are performed. It would be helpful if there were a table
containing all compounds tested, and Ki values for each replicate performed. I'm not suggesting all compounds require
multiple replicates but claims in the text should be robustly supported when differences are small, such as 5.10 nM for
nirmatrelvir and 3.08 nM for FD3-6. Take care to explain if biological replicates or technical replicates have been performed.
Minor points:
1) Can the authors elaborate why Nirmatrelvir always outperforms FD3-x series in brain tissue? Is this because of blood-
brain barrier or the chemical properties of FD3-x series after introducing the pyridine/iso-quinoline?
2) Line 11-14, Page 26 is at odds with Line 10, Page 5. Actually, GISAID data only indicates 10-1000 counts of E166 escape
variants out of more than 10 million counts. Is there literature to support the claim that these variants are "becoming
increasingly prevalent".
3) Line 11, Page 28. The study shows that only E166A can be inhibited by FD3-x compounds in the nM range, while E166V
is µM range. The claims around E166 should be limited to those variants that have been tested.
4) Page 12 - SAR section. Please clarify the nature of the assay used to determine Ki values. I assume this is the enzymatic
assay with peptide substrate as described in the methods, but as NMR could potentially be used to extract binding by
chemical shift perturbations, it would be helpful to clarify this in the main text.
5) The "Enamine" Library is not defined. This company sells many libraries.

### Reviewer 3

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 4

The comments below are on the pharmacokinetics of the developed antiviral compounds reported in this manuscript. The
developed compounds appear to present pharmacokinetic improvements over current compounds. However the evaluation
of the data and interpretation of the results should be based on applying the pharmacokinetic principles and should be
biologically meaningful.
Page 6, lines 13-15 and elsewhere in the manuscript: Improved pharmacokinetic properties are not linked to enhancement
of in vitro efficacy because pharmacokinetics are related to processes in the body and not reactions that happen in vitro. The
manuscript also mixes principles of PK with potency. Correct representation of the terminology and underlying basic
concepts would be beneficial.
Page 19 and Figure S20: The manuscript claims that FD3-32 has a longer PO t1/2 compared to IV t1/2, however Figure S20
suggests that this conclusion may be based on a 10-fold differences in dose amounts and on a lack of measurement at 24 h
for the IV dose, potentially due to the limit of quantification. Based on pharmacokinetic principles, the elimination half-life is
not affected by the route of administration, unless there is a rare case of flip-flop kinetics which appears not to be the
case here (and if it was, it needs to discussed). Rather, the difference in half-lives appears to be an artifact of comparing
different dose levels with the concentrations following the lower (IV) dose falling below the limit of quantification much
earlier. Contemporary PK modelling approaches can account for samples below the quantification limit.
Figure S20: How many samples in the FD3-32 panel were measurable at 24 h (given no error bar is visible) and if not all of
them, how were the others treated in the analysis? Simply leaving out samples with concentrations below the limit of
quantification can substantially bias the conclusions and comparisons.
Tables S2 and S3: The SD or %CV should be reported not only the average of the parameter estimates.
Elimination half-life is not a primary PK parameter but it is a composite parameter which is determined by elimination
clearance and volume of distribution which are the primary biological PK parameters. Therefore, meaningful comparisons
should be based on clearance and volume of distribution and not primarily on elimination half-life.
Page 22, lines 14-16: This is not really a biologically informed statement because elimination t1/2 is a composite parameter
of the biological PK parameters elimination clearance and volume of distribution, whereas bioavailability is related to the
extent absorbed. It would be more informative to evaluate which underlying biological processes are affected by the different
structures of the compounds.

### Reviewer 5

The following comments are made from the reviewer’s expertise in NMR.
1. The resolution of Figure S9A should be increased to ensure that peak assignments are clearly visible.
2. The TROSY-HSQC spectrum in Figure S9 shows noticeable noise peaks and peak clusters compared with previously
reported spectra (Figure S9A). This suggests that the protein sample used in this study has some solubility issue or
folding problem. The authors state that assignments were made according to published data. To substantiate this, the reported
spectrum should be directly overlaid with the spectrum collected in this study, using distinct colors. Additionally,
assignments from the BMRB should be mapped directly onto the newly collected spectrum. This step is essential because
many peaks claimed to undergo CSP overlap with nearby signals, making the assignments potentially ambiguous. For
example, assignments of residues such as V171 and T175 appear reliable, whereas those of G170, V186, V42, and Q192 are
ambiguous due to crowding (Fig. 2). Similarly, L141, N142, and E166 assignments are unreliable because of severe
overlap.
3. The authors report that upon inhibitor addition, NMR peaks become sharper (Fig. S10). However, peak line-shape
changes should be presented more objectively, for example, by displaying normalized 1D slices. Apparent differences in
contour maps can be misleading because they depend on the contour level chosen.

### Reviewer 6

The manuscript by Gan Luo et al. presents an integrative approach to develop new inhibitors against SARS-CoV-2 Mpro
with an emphasis on tackling the main drawbacks of the approved Paxlovid. While the manuscript is overall well written,
some language editing could be helpful as strange use of words appear in various places. The amount of data and evidence
of the superior characteristics of the new compounds is impressive and warrants publication in Nat Commun. It is however
hard to assess all methods and per request of the editor, the focus is here on the presented mass spectrometry data, for
which I have just a few comments.
Major comments:
- Figures are on the small end and would benefit from enlarging. The supplementary figures are in part better but e.g. S2 is
also very small, it is impossible to read the labels in the structures.
- None of the compounds shows the expected occupancy in MS reflecting nM affinities. What is the mechanism of covalent
attachment? Can the chemistry be reverted under the experimental workflow? Since the authors have performed titrations, it
is advisable to use quantitation rather than just saying it recapitulates the other data. Please also mention in legend of Fig. 4
what concentrations have been used, so it is possible to compare to Fig. S16.
Minor:
- p.3 l.17 the processed proteins are implicated in replication, whether some may also play a role in assembly, suggest to
rephrase.
- with three replicates reporting SD is usually suboptimal and SEM is to be preferred as statistics are insufficient to determine
a standard deviation
- please order supplementary figures in order of appearance. Fig. S5 should be shown much later. If it is shown at that place
for the WT, then it would be worthwhile showing that with S8 and mention that this is to prove the 15N incorporation, which is
currently not the case.
- Fig. S8 - please mention/label that this is WT Mpro
- Fig. 4 and S15 - please provide the calculated mass of the inhibitors next to the compound in Fig. S15 as well. Importantly
also provide the absolute concentrations (at least in the figure legends) as these determine bound fractions. Just providing a
ratio is misleading.
Supplement p.15 ESI-MS
-please specify the mass spectrometer and software used for deconvolution
-is the elution profile of free Mpro and inhibitor-modified Mpro identical? If not, this may explain the high fraction of
unmodified Mpro in Figs. 4 and S16.

### Reviewer 7

This study combines computational and experimental methods to develop improved SARS-CoV-2 Mpro inhibitors that
overcome drug resistance and pharmacokinetic limitations associated with Paxlovid. Through structure-based virtual
screening, molecular dynamics simulations, and both in vitro and in vivo testing, the authors identify iso-quinoline-based
peptidomimetics with good antiviral activity and pharmacokinetic properties. The compounds offer a promising new scaffold
and contribute to the goal of pan-coronavirus antiviral development, since they show activity against both SARS-CoV-1 and
MERS-CoV. The approach is rational, integrating computational tools and experiments for compound testing and validation
of in silico predictions.
Validation of the docking protocol through redocking of known ligands to the target (e.g. positive control testing) is a standard
best practice that appears to be missing. Such validation confirms that the docking setup can accurately reproduce
experimentally observed binding poses for target under study and supports confidence in the screening results. If this step
was performed but omitted from the writeup for brevity, including it would strengthen confidence in the docking approach and
serve as a reference for other researchers who may work on Mpro inhibitor development in the future.
Line 17 on Page 6 in the Supplementary Information appears to repeat the initial lines of the Molecular Docking section.
Separating multiple docking methods into clearly defined subsections would improve clarity and reproducibility.
The authors mention using Epik and PROPKA to assign protonation states at pH 7, but they do not specify selected
protonation states. Histidine can be sensitive to local environment including at pH 7, besides the choice of epsilon versus
delta hydrogen when neutral. These chemical-level details can be important for understanding ligand binding preferences if
titratable residues occur in the antiviral binding site.
Given extensive experimental testing and validation, including in vitro enzymatic and antiviral assays, pharmacokinetics,
and in vivo efficacy in infected mice, results of the study are compelling, and concerns related to computational methodology
are minor.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

It remains elusive to design peptidomimetic inhibitors of SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro) refractory to multiple deficiencies of Paxlovid (ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir), pertaining mainly to E166X mutations-conferred drug resistance and inherent pharmacokinetic limitations to nirmatrelvir. We identify via virtual screening an iso-quinoline P1 moiety in place of the traditional γ-lactam and design iso-quinoline-containing inhibitors with high affinity for Mpro and its nirmatrelvir-resistant E166X mutants. Further optimization at P4 cultivates distinctive peptidomimetic inhibitors with drastically improved pharmacokinetic properties and significantly enhanced antiviral efficacy independent of ritonavir. Two such inhibitors, FD3-32 and FD3-36, also potent against SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV Mpro, are more effective as a monotherapy regimen than Paxlovid in reducing viral loads in vivo and protecting infected male mice from acute lung injury. Here, we report the discovery of next-generation SARS-CoV-2 Mpro inhibitors that overcome the deficiencies of Paxlovid, promising efficacious antivirals critical for mitigating the current and future pandemics of coronaviruses.

---

## Introduction

Within a short period of two decades, the world has already succumbed to three major pandemics of coronaviruses with grave human sufferings, i.e., severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 1 (SARS-CoV-1) in 2003 1, Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) in 2012 2, and, particularly, SARS-CoV-2 that causes coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) 3. Tens of millions of people have died worldwide from COVID-19 since December 2019 4, and many more patients who survived SARS-CoV-2 infection have, without timely antiviral intervention, suffered long COVID – a collection of long-lasting symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, brain fog, etc 5. The ritonavir (RTV)-boosted oral antiviral nirmatrelvir (NTV), i.e., Paxlovid, developed by Pfizer as a peptidomimetic inhibitor of SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro or 3CLpro), has saved millions of lives globally, and is chiefly responsible, along with mRNA vaccination, for largely mitigating the COVID-19 pandemic.

SARS-CoV-2 Mpro is a cysteine protease that processes viral polyproteins important for the assembly and replication of the positive-sense single-stranded RNA β-coronavirus 3,6-9. Mpro operates the Cys145-His41 catalytic dyad in its active cleft to cleave protein substrates at the specific site of GlnP1-XxxP1’ 7-9; this P1-restricted substrate specificity differs from that of known human cysteine proteases 8,10, making SARS-CoV-2 Mpro an ideal drug target for antiviral therapy 10. Numerous Mpro inhibitors of different structural classes have been reported 11,12, among which NTV, a rationally designed peptidomimetic covalent inhibitor with a γ-lactam ring (formed intramolecularly between the α-amino and side-chain amide groups of Gln) at P1 position 13, and ensitrelvir (ETV), a non-covalent small-molecule inhibitor derived through structure-based virtual screening 14, are clinically proven to be highly effective antivirals for the treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infections.

Despite the huge initial success achieved by Paxlovid in mitigating the COVID-19 pandemic, two major deficiencies of the antiviral are emerging, including evolved drug resistance and adverse clinical effects posed by RTV. The γ-lactam ring at P1 is a general molecular signature of most peptidomimetic covalent inhibitors of Mpro as it supersedes Gln side chain with reduced conformational entropy and, thus, improved binding affinity for the viral protease 15,16. In fact, a network of three H-bonds formed by the P1 residue, Gln side chain or γ-lactam ring, with the three residues F140, H163 and E166 lining part of the S1 binding pocket is strictly maintained in both peptide substrate-Mpro and NTV-Mpro complexes (Figure 1a and Figure S1), structurally validating the “canonical” γ-lactam-for-Gln design strategy. When a six-membered δ-lactam ring was introduced at P1 of nirmatrelvir, a stronger H-bond formed between the lactam NH and E166 side chain carboxylate, largely responsible for several-fold enhancement of inhibitory and antiviral activity 17. While this high-fidelity H-bonding network involving the side chains of H163 Nε2 and E166 Oε2 ensures recognition specificity in both catalysis and inhibition, it invites escape mutations at these two positions for the virus to develop drug resistance. A recent study has shown that an H163A mutation completely abolishes the catalytic activity of Mpro due to mutation-induced conformational changes 18, leaving E166 all the more vulnerable to either laboratory-evolved or clinically selected mutations for potential resistance 19-22. In fact, drug-resistant variants of the virus featuring E166A or E166V mutation in Mpro, often in combination with M49L, L50F and/or L167F compensatory mutations to partially improve replicative fitness 19, exhibit much-reduced sensitivity to NTV and/or ETV due mainly to the loss of electrostatic interactions afforded by E166 side chain 19,23-27. Although the prevalence of E166X mutations is relatively low in clinical strains 21, pre-emptive and sharply focused efforts are warranted to develop peptidomimetic inhibitors of Mpro with a “non-canonical” P1 moiety to maximally circumvent drug resistance conferred by E166 mutations.

Adverse clinical effects posed by RTV are perhaps a more imminent threat to the future success of Paxlovid, which brought in for Pfizer $5.7B revenues in 2024 alone 28. RTV is an HIV-1 protease inhibitor clinically used along with other drugs for the treatment of HIV-1 infection 29,30. Coincidentally, RTV also potently inhibits cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), an enzyme in the liver that metabolizes NTV primarily through oxidation of the γ-lactam ring 13, and P-glycoprotein (P-gp), a multidrug efflux transporter in the plasma membrane that diminishes intracellular NTV 31. While co-administration of RTV significantly improves therapeutic efficacy of NTV against SARS-CoV-2 infection by suppressing hepatic metabolism and drug efflux 32, it poses serious concerns of drug-drug interactions with multiple medications even after withdrawal of Paxlovid 33,34, thus adversely affecting the treatment of other diseases 31,34,35. For this reason, earnest efforts are ongoing to develop efficacious antiviral monotherapy against SARS-CoV-2 infection without RTV 36,37.

In this work, we initially set out to tackle evolved drug resistance to NTV through the discovery of a distinctive class of peptidomimetic inhibitors against SARS-CoV-2 Mpro and its E166X mutants. We find that iso-quinoline in place of γ-lactam ring at P1 largely overcome drug resistance instigated by E166X mutations. Additional modifications at P4 improve pharmacokinetic properties of these inhibitors, which leads in a monotherapy to enhanced in vivo antiviral efficacy compared with NTV (with or without RTV). Further, these inhibitors are potently active against Mpro from SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV, promising a next generation of broad-spectrum antivirals with far reaching implications for clinical intervention of future pandemics of sarbecoviruses and merbecoviruses.
